hints: Look closely at the AB row in the table. What antigens does this recipient have, and more importantly, what antibodies are in their plasma?

Remember the transfusion rule given: agglutination happens only if the recipient has an antibody that matches the donor antigen. So check if an AB recipient has any antibody to attack A or B antigens.
walkthrough:
**Identify the recipient**

Look at the table for blood group AB. Their red cells carry both A and B antigens, but their plasma contains neither antibody. This is the key starting point.

**Apply the safe transfusion rule**

A transfusion is unsafe only if the recipient's antibody attacks the donor's antigen. Since the AB recipient has no anti-A and no anti-B antibodies, they cannot attack any ABO donor cells.

**Check all donor groups**

Donor A has A antigen, donor B has B antigen, donor AB has A and B, donor O has neither. None of these will be attacked by an AB recipient, so all four groups can be given safely. That gives answer D.

options.A: Too narrow. AB blood is safe, but AB recipients can also accept other groups because they have no antibodies to attack them.
options.B: Too narrow. Group O is safe because it has no antigens, but AB recipients can also accept A, B and AB for the same reason.
options.C: Incomplete. A and B are both safe for an AB recipient, but AB and O are also safe, so this misses two valid donors.
options.D: Correct. An AB recipient has neither antibody, so no donor A or B antigen will be attacked. This makes AB the universal recipient for the ABO system.
